title: Living stones (1 Peter 2:1–10)
hook: you are living stones built into a spiritual house
tomorrow: what do you say when a friend asks why you even believe?

segments.voice: A living hope, born through the resurrection, honest about heaviness, tried like gold. The King James called it lively. Hold on to that odd word, because it's back today.
screen: `A LIVING HOPE.` → `LIVELY: THE ODD WORD IS BACK.`

segments.voice: Stones don't breathe. They don't grow, or choose where they go; they sit where someone sets them. So 1 Peter says something that sounds like a mistake: "Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house." Lively stones. Living ones. How can a stone be alive? The letter has already given the clue, a few words earlier, and it starts with one particular stone: the one the builders threw away.
screen: `STONES DON'T BREATHE.` → `LIVELY STONES?` → `THE ONE THEY THREW AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the clue. Jesus is "a living stone, disallowed indeed of men, but chosen of God, and precious." Rejected, put to death, and alive again: that's yesterday's living hope, turned into stone. Then the letter quotes an old song: "the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner." The reject ends up holding the walls together. So here's the puzzle solved. The stones are alive because the stone they're built on is alive. People come to him, and they're fitted in around him, and the house grows. And look at the shape of it: not bricks pressed from one mold, all the same size, but stones, each its own shape, each with a place. Then the house needs priests, and the letter calls the readers "a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people." Peculiar, in the King James, means belonging to God, not strange. Churches read the royal priesthood in their own ways. Protestant teaching speaks of the priesthood of all believers. Catholic and Orthodox teaching says all the baptized share in Christ's priesthood, alongside ordained priests who serve at the altar. And then the line that holds it together: "Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God." Loose stones, now a house.
screen: `A LIVING STONE, REJECTED.` · `THE REJECT HOLDS THE CORNER.` · `NO TWO STONES ALIKE.` · `A ROYAL PRIESTHOOD, READ TWO WAYS.` · then, large: `LIVING STONES.`

segments.voice: Pick up something small and solid: a stone if there's one nearby, or a key or a coin. Close your hand around it and feel its weight and its edges, the shape that's only its own. For the sit, let it stand for one stone set into something bigger than itself.
Living stones. First Peter, chapter two: people built up into a spiritual house around the living stone the builders rejected.
Keep this one: living stones, each a different shape and all of them in the wall. Be well.

chat.says: dad's crew built pop a ramp. nia painted. i just held boards. pop says 'living stones.' do i count?
options: Yes. Peter's stones aren't one mold; each fits its own place. Holding boards is a stone's job.
Not really. In 1 Peter only the cornerstone matters; the other stones are just filler.
Only if you're ordained. Peter's royal priesthood means the church's leaders, not helpers.
chat.meaning: 1 Peter pictures lively stones built up into one spiritual house around the living stone. Every stone has a place, not only the big ones.

disallowed.meaning: the King James word for rejected

head of the corner.meaning: the key stone where two walls meet, or the capstone

priesthood.meaning: people set apart to serve God and offer worship

peculiar.meaning: in the King James, belonging to God, not strange

Orthodox.meaning: the Eastern Orthodox churches, such as Greek and Russian

v3 puzzle shape: the odd detail is 'lively stones' (stones that are alive); the solution is that the stones are built on the living stone (2:4), rejected and alive again. 'Alive again' links to the resurrection named in 1:3; confirm the reading.

'The letter quotes an old song': 1 Peter 2:7 does not name the psalm; the match to Psalm 118:22 is the standard cross-reference. The screen says 'the reject holds the corner'; the gloss notes the cornerstone/capstone question.
'Peculiar, in the King James, means belonging to God' is a word-meaning claim; please confirm.

Where churches differ: Protestant teaching (priesthood of all believers) and Catholic and Orthodox teaching (common priesthood of the baptized alongside ordained priests) are stated without ranking. Please confirm the wording is fair to each.
'Nothing says one mold' (myth reveal) describes the text's silence, not a claim it makes.
